U.S. Supreme Court · No. 24‑656 · D.C. Circuit · No. 24‑1113 TikTok v. Garland In April 2024 Congress gave ByteDance, TikTok’s China-based parent company, until January 19, 2025 to sell the app’s US business, or app stores and web hosts in the United States would have to drop it. TikTok and a group of creators sued, saying the law broke the First Amendment. On January 17, 2025, the Supreme Court upheld it, and no justice dissented. Then the law wasn’t enforced. The new President held it off five times and approved a sale, and a new company took over in January 2026. A new case says that sale breaks the same law, and it’s still open. Filed May 7, 2024 Argued Jan 10, 2025 Decided Jan 17, 2025 Status Law upheld

Petitioners The side that asked the court to step in The app’s US company and its China-based parent TikTok Inc. is the California company that runs the app in the United States. Two companies further up, it’s owned by ByteDance Ltd., which is incorporated in the Cayman Islands and has its main operations in China. ByteDance owns the recommendation algorithm, which is developed and maintained in China. Its founder, Zhang Yiming, a Chinese national, owns 21 percent. Eight people who post on TikTok sued too, in a case of their own heard alongside this one: Brian Firebaugh, a rancher and Marine veteran, Chloe Joy Sexton, Talia Cadet, Timothy Martin, Paul Tran, Steven King, Kiera Spann and Christopher Townsend. They post about ranching, parenting and a cookie business, books, football, skincare, sober living, survivors of sexual assault, and music and faith. BASED Politics, a nonprofit that makes videos for Gen Z, joined them. Noel Francisco, a former Solicitor General, argued for TikTok in the Supreme Court, and Jeffrey Fisher for the creators. Andrew Pincus argued for TikTok in the D.C. Circuit. D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 10–11 · Opinion p. 3 · Creators’ brief pp. 5–7 · Tr. p. 2 · Jones Day, Francisco · D.C. Cir. opinion p. 1

Respondent The side answering Attorney General, sued in that role The law gives the job of enforcing it to the Attorney General and no one else, so the Attorney General was the one sued, in that role and not as a person. Garland held the office until President Biden’s term ended on January 20, 2025, and the Supreme Court’s case keeps his name. The office has since passed to Pamela Bondi, and in April 2026 to Todd Blanche, who was confirmed in August 2026. Elizabeth Prelogar, the Solicitor General, argued for the government in the Supreme Court, and Daniel Tenny of the Justice Department in the D.C. Circuit. Its evidence was mostly sworn statements from officials of the intelligence agencies, the FBI and the Justice Department. Some of it was classified, and neither court relied on that part. Pub. L. 118-50 § 2(d) · Tr. p. 2 · D.C. Cir. opinion p. 3 · Amended petition ¶ 17 · States Newsroom, Aug 8, 2026

Two cases were heard together the whole way. TikTok and ByteDance’s is No. 24-1113 in the D.C. Circuit and No. 24-656 in the Supreme Court. The creators’ is No. 24-1130 and No. 24-657, Firebaugh v. Garland. A third petition, BASED Politics’, No. 24-1183, was joined to them in the D.C. Circuit. One opinion in each court decided them all. Other challenges to the same law are left out. The Supreme Court’s case is over. It sent its judgment down on February 18, 2025, and the D.C. Circuit closed the case ten days later. What happened to the law after that, the orders not to enforce it, the sale and the new company, happened outside both courts, and these pages say so card by card. Then in March 2026 a new case was filed under the same law, Tan v. Trump, No. 26-1047 in the D.C. Circuit. Two software engineers who own stock in Alphabet and Meta brought it, and later a former employee of a ByteDance company, against President Trump and the Attorney General. It says the sale isn’t the one the law demands. It’s still open. These pages show it as far as its record goes, with what each side says marked as what that side says. Judgment issued · Mandate, Feb 28, 2025 · Docket, No. 26-1047 · Amended petition ¶¶ 13–15

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. The Supreme Court upheld the law as it applies to TikTok and the creators. Trump say about the deal is reported as their claim, and the President’s findings about it as his findings. The government also filed classified evidence that TikTok never saw. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in Washington. The law sends every challenge to it first, and to no other court.
The three judges of an appeals court who hear a case or a motion. The D.C. Circuit has about a dozen judges, and different panels handle different steps.
The panel that will decide a case itself, as opposed to the ones that handle motions along the way.
The head of the Justice Department. The law gives this office alone the job of enforcing it, which is why the case is named after one.
The lawyer who argues the federal government’s cases in the Supreme Court. Elizabeth Prelogar held the job when this case was argued.

The court’s numbered list of everything filed in a case. Entry 42 is the forty-second thing filed.

The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, the federal panel that reviews foreign purchases of US businesses for security risks.

The part of the Constitution that bars the government from “abridging the freedom of speech.” Courts check laws that burden speech with one of a few tests.
A court treating something as true for the sake of argument, because the answer wouldn’t change the result, and leaving the real question open.
Any of the stricter tests a court uses when a law burdens speech, instead of just asking whether the law is reasonable.
The hardest test. The government needs a compelling reason and the narrowest way of getting there. Most laws that get it fail.
The middle test. The government needs an important reason that isn’t about suppressing speech, and a law that doesn’t burden much more speech than it has to.
Aimed at what is said, its topic, idea or message. A content-based law gets strict scrutiny.
Applying whatever is said, like a limit on how loud a speaker can be. A content-neutral law gets intermediate scrutiny.
A law aimed at one speaker. Courts look harder when that’s a way of getting at what the speaker says.
Whether a law fits its reason, covering what the problem needs and not much more.
Another way of meeting the same goal that burdens less speech. If one would work as well, the law can fail.
Covering too little of the problem a law claims to fix, which can suggest the stated reason isn’t the real one.
A court giving weight to another branch’s judgment, here Congress’s predictions about national security.
The government’s second reason: that China could secretly have ByteDance change what Americans see on TikTok. The Supreme Court didn’t rest on it.
The Constitution’s promise that the government won’t treat people differently without a good enough reason.
A law that punishes a named person or group without a trial. The Constitution forbids Congress to pass one.
The government seizing private property, which the Constitution allows only with fair payment.
The right to bring a case at all. A challenger has to show a real injury of their own, caused by what they’re challenging, that a court could fix.

Does the First Amendment even apply to this law?
The first fight · Speech, or just ownership?

Before any test can apply Assumed so · Jan 17, 2025 This is where the government started. The law doesn’t ban any video or tell anyone what to say, it argued. It only says who can own TikTok, and ByteDance, a foreign company abroad, has no free-speech rights to begin with. If that’s right, there’s no First Amendment question at all, and the law just has to be reasonable. TikTok and the creators said the law shuts down an American company’s speech and 170 million people’s place to post, so of course it applies. The D.C. Circuit agreed with them on this. The Supreme Court didn’t decide it. It assumed the First Amendment applies and moved on, which basically means the law passes even if TikTok is right about this part. Justice Sotomayor would have said yes outright. What each side said The government: a foreign company can’t use “an American puppet as a mouthpiece.” TikTok: “It’s a burden on TikTok’s speech, so the First Amendment applies.”

Outcome Then The law just has to be reasonable That’s the outcome the government asked for first. A law about who owns a company, with no First Amendment question in it, would almost certainly stand. Neither court went this way. The D.C. Circuit said the First Amendment applies, and the Supreme Court left the question open.
Is the law aimed at what people say?
Which test? · The hardest one or the middle one

What the test turns on No · content-neutral, Jan 17, 2025 Courts test speech laws harder or easier depending on what they’re aimed at. A law aimed at what people say, its topic or its message, is content-based, and it gets strict scrutiny, the hardest test, which most laws fail. A law that applies whatever is said is content-neutral, and it only gets the middle test, intermediate scrutiny. So this is the fight over which test applies, and the two cards inside it are the two ways TikTok said the law is aimed at speech. Either one would have been enough. The case goes on to the test either way, but the answer here decides how hard that test is. A yes on either one is enough or
Does the law pick out apps by what’s on them?
Part one · The words of the law

No · not as applied, Jan 17, 2025 The law’s general rule only covers apps where people post and share their own content, and it leaves out apps whose main purpose is reviews of products, businesses or travel. TikTok said that makes the whole law content-based from the start. The Supreme Court said that part doesn’t matter here. The review-site exclusion only applies to the law’s general track, and TikTok was named in the law itself. Looking only at TikTok’s part, the law is about who controls the app, not what’s on it.
Is the law’s reason about content?
Part two · The reason for the law

No · the data reason isn’t, Jan 17, 2025 The government gave two reasons. One is data, that China could collect information on 170 million Americans. The other is covert content manipulation, that China could secretly push ByteDance to change what Americans see. TikTok said the second one is about content, plain and simple. The Court called the data reason “decidedly content agnostic.” It didn’t decide whether the second one is about content, because it found Congress would have passed the law for the data reason alone. Justice Gorsuch wrote that he had “serious reservations” about calling the law content-neutral, but he agreed with the result.
Is the government’s reason important enough?
The test, part one · The reason

Why the government wanted it Yes · the data reason alone, Jan 17, 2025 Under the middle test the government needs an important reason, and under the hardest one a compelling one. Here that means its two reasons, data and covert manipulation. If either one is strong enough, the law gets past this card. TikTok and the creators said a government can’t act because of what people might be persuaded of, so the manipulation reason doesn’t count at all. On data they mostly argued that this law doesn’t fit it, which is the next card. The Supreme Court decided this card on data alone. A yes on either one is enough or
Is keeping Americans’ data away from China a strong enough reason?

Yes · Jan 17, 2025 The government said TikTok collects huge amounts of personal data, on its users and on people in their contacts who never signed up, and that China’s laws can make ByteDance hand it over. Its lawyer pointed to China’s past hacks of federal personnel files, Equifax and Anthem. “Petitioners do not dispute” that this interest is important, the Court wrote. “Nor could they.” Even the creators’ lawyer said at argument that data security “is compelling.” The D.C. Circuit called it compelling too.
Can the government act to stop China secretly steering what Americans see?

Not decided This is the reason TikTok said is forbidden. The creators’ lawyer put it this way at argument: restricting speech “because it might sow doubt about our leaders or undermine democracy” is what “our enemies do.” The government said it isn’t about any message, it’s about a foreign adversary having that power at all. The D.C. Circuit said this reason was compelling too. The Supreme Court didn’t decide it. Justice Gorsuch wrote that “One man’s ‘covert content manipulation’ is another’s ‘editorial discretion,’” and said the Court was right not to rest on it.

Outcome Then Its reason wasn’t enough If neither reason were strong enough, the part of the law that names TikTok couldn’t be enforced, and ByteDance could keep TikTok. That’s where TikTok wanted the case to end. It didn’t, because the data reason alone was enough for every judge and justice.
Is a forced sale more than the problem needs?
The test, part two · The fit

Whether a smaller fix would do No · Jan 17, 2025 Even with a good reason, a law can’t burden a lot more speech than it needs to. That’s tailoring. TikTok offered smaller fixes, each one, it said, a less restrictive alternative: the 90-page security agreement it had negotiated, with Oracle checking the code, a ban on sharing users’ data with anyone, or a warning label on the app. The government said none of them would work, because it couldn’t trust ByteDance or watch it closely enough. The Court sided with the government. The law isn’t an outright ban, it said, but “a conditional ban,” lifted the moment China’s control ends, and the alternatives “do not alter our tailoring analysis.” It gave deference to Congress’s judgment about national security.

Outcome Then A smaller fix would have done If a smaller fix would have worked as well, the forced sale would fail the test, and the part of the law that names TikTok couldn’t be enforced. The Court didn’t go there. It said Congress could reasonably decide that only a sale would do.
Does the law break the Constitution any other way?
Only the appeals court answered these · Dec 6, 2024

TikTok’s other three claims No, all three · Dec 6, 2024 TikTok also said the law breaks three other parts of the Constitution. The D.C. Circuit turned down all three. The Supreme Court only agreed to answer the free-speech question, so these were decided once, by the appeals court, and that’s where they stand. Any one of them would have been enough to stop the law, so a yes on any card inside this one would have meant TikTok won. A yes on any one is enough or or
Did Congress single TikTok out unfairly?

No · Dec 6, 2024 TikTok said Congress treated it worse than every other app without a good enough reason, which would break the Constitution’s promise of equal protection. The court said Congress had its reasons. “The Act singled out TikTok because of its known characteristics and history.”
Is the law a punishment without a trial?

No · Dec 6, 2024 The Constitution bars Congress from passing a bill of attainder, a law that punishes a named person or group without a trial. TikTok said a law naming it is exactly that. The court said the law asks for “a sale, not a confiscation,” and leaves the way out open forever. The government’s effort, it wrote, “reflects a forward-looking prophylactic, not a backward-looking punitive, purpose.”
Does the law take TikTok’s property without paying for it?

No · Dec 6, 2024 The government can take private property only if it pays fairly for it. TikTok said forcing a sale, maybe at a fire-sale price, is a taking. The court said the problem was China. Its export rules were what made a sale hard, and “the PRC, not the divestiture offramp in the Act, is the source of TikTok’s difficulty.”

Outcome Then On other grounds A win on any of these would have stopped the part of the law that names TikTok, whatever the free-speech answer was. None got that far, and the Supreme Court never looked at them.

Outcome Then ByteDance has until January 19, 2025 This is where the case ended. Every judge and justice agreed the law could be enforced. ByteDance had until January 19, 2025 to sell, or app stores and web hosts in the US would have to drop TikTok. What happened next wasn’t up to a court. It’s the chain below.

Not a question for a court No · Jan 20, 2025 onward This one wasn’t decided by a court. Only the Attorney General can enforce this law, and it took effect the day before President Trump took office. TikTok shut itself off for about half a day, then came back on his promise. On his first day he ordered the Attorney General not to enforce it, and he renewed that order four times. The Justice Department wrote to Apple, Google and the rest promising them no liability. That was non-enforcement, not the law’s own extension, and it’s part of what Tan v. Trump challenges.

Outcome Then App stores and web hosts drop TikTok That’s what the law said would happen on January 19, 2025 unless TikTok was sold first. Any company that kept offering it would face fines of up to $5,000 for each US user. It’s roughly what the challengers in Tan v. Trump say the law required then, though they aren’t asking for a ban now.
Does the 2026 sale break the law?

The case is here The case after the case Undecided The law only lifts the ban after a qualified divestiture, a sale that leaves no operational relationship with ByteDance. President Trump decided on September 25, 2025 that this deal is one, and the new company took over on January 22, 2026. Two software engineers, later joined by a former ByteDance employee, say it isn’t, and they’ve asked the D.C. Circuit to say so. Before the court gets to the deal itself, it has two questions about the challengers, and the government says they lose on both. The challengers need a yes on all three cards inside this one. The court hasn’t ruled on any of them. On July 20, 2026 it sent the first two on to the judges who will decide the whole case. A yes to all three is needed and and

Undecided The law gives 90 days to challenge a government action, a deadline to sue. The government says the last action was the President’s order of September 25, 2025, so the March 2026 petition “missed by several months.” The challengers say that order only approved the deal “once its implementation agreements are executed,” so nothing was final until the sale closed on January 22, and they sued “a few weeks later.” The government says the only thing that happened in January was the President’s post about it, which isn’t an order.
Can these challengers sue at all?

Undecided To bring a case you need standing, a real harm of your own. The challengers say Reid uses TikTok and his data is still shared with ByteDance, that Doe lost his job in the deal, and that Tan and Reid lost money as shareholders in TikTok’s rivals. The government says shareholders can’t sue over harm to their companies, that the effect on stock prices is “highly speculative,” and that the data claim is “speculation piled upon speculation.”

Undecided This is the heart of it. The challengers say ByteDance still owns the algorithm and licenses it to the new company, still runs its e-commerce, advertising and marketing, and that TikTok’s global chief executive sits on its board. They say ByteDance staff still get US user data. Those are their claims, and none has been tested. The government hasn’t argued this part yet. Its view so far is the President’s own findings, that the new company controls the algorithms, the code and moderation, keeps US data in an American company’s cloud, and has the algorithm retrained on US data.

Outcome Then The Attorney General has to investigate That’s what the challengers ask for, a ruling that the extensions, the failure to investigate and the sale broke the law, and an order for the Attorney General to investigate. They don’t ask the court to ban TikTok. What would follow isn’t clear. The law leaves enforcement, and its fines, to the Attorney General.

Outcome Then TikTok stays with the new company If the challengers sued too late or can’t sue at all, the case ends without any court ruling on the deal itself. If the court does rule on the deal and finds it meets the law, the sale is settled. Either way, the new company keeps running TikTok in the US, as it has since January 2026.

Every card comes from the court record, the law or the President’s orders, or from a report that says what the record doesn’t. The cards on the shutdown weekend, the letters and the deal rely on reporting, and say so.
This wasn’t the first try. The government had been worried about TikTok since 2018, and two Presidents had tried to deal with it.
TikTok comes to the United States

Having bought the lip-sync app Musical.ly, ByteDance, a Chinese tech company, merges it into TikTok and relaunches the app here. That purchase is where the government’s worries start. The D.C. Circuit dates the first of them to 2018, when the merged app was relaunched in the US. It grew fast. In 2023 alone, the Supreme Court later wrote, people in the US uploaded more than 5.5 billion videos to it, viewed more than 13 trillion times. D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 11–12 · Order of Aug 14, 2020 · Opinion p. 2
President Trump orders TikTok banned, then sold

On August 6 he bans dealings with ByteDance under an emergency law. On August 14 he orders it to sell TikTok’s US business. The first order said TikTok “automatically captures vast swaths of information from its users,” and that China could use it to “track the locations of Federal employees and contractors, build dossiers of personal information for blackmail, and conduct corporate espionage.” It relied on IEEPA, a 1977 emergency powers law. The second followed a review by CFIUS, which had concluded on August 1 that the risks of the Musical.ly purchase couldn’t be fixed short of a sale. EO 13942 · Order of Aug 14, 2020 · D.C. Cir. opinion p. 12

TikTok and a group of creators sue, and federal judges in Washington and Pennsylvania stop the ban from taking effect. The judges found the emergency law didn’t reach “personal communication” or “informational materials,” which Congress had written out of it. The government appealed, then dropped the appeals in 2021. TikTok also challenged the order to sell, in the D.C. Circuit, on November 10, 2020. That case was put on hold in February 2021 while the two sides negotiated. TikTok’s petition ¶¶ 19–22 · D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 12–13

A new order replaces Trump’s with a wider review of apps tied to foreign adversaries. The order to sell stays. Biden’s order named China as “a foreign adversary,” and said apps like these could give one “vast swaths of information from users.” He asked his agencies for options, including laws Congress could pass. EO 14034 · D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 12–13
A 90-page deal that was never signed

TikTok negotiates a national security agreement with CFIUS to keep US data away from ByteDance, with Oracle checking the code. By TikTok’s count there were at least 14 meetings or calls, nine written presentations and 15 rounds of email. The plan put US data in a separate company, TikTok U.S. Data Security, stored with Oracle, which would also inspect the source code. It even let the government shut the app off in the US in some cases, which TikTok calls a “kill switch.” TikTok sent its last proposal in August 2022. It built much of the plan anyway, calling it Project Texas, and says it spent more than $2 billion on it. D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 13–15 · TikTok’s petition ¶ 8

Congress bars TikTok from federal government devices, in the year-end spending law. That law, the No TikTok on Government Devices Act, is still on the books. In 2026 the Justice Department decided it doesn’t cover the new TikTok. Pub. L. 117-328, div. R · D.C. Cir. opinion p. 13

After months of silence, TikTok says, CFIUS tells it ByteDance will have to sell the US business. That’s TikTok’s account, in its petition. The government’s is that the draft agreement wasn’t enough. Some US data would still flow to China, ByteDance could still control the app, and the government couldn’t trust it or watch it closely enough. “In the Executive’s view,” the D.C. Circuit wrote, “divestment was the only solution.” TikTok’s petition ¶ 24 · D.C. Cir. opinion p. 15
Seven weeks from bill to law.

Eight days after the bill was introduced. It gives ByteDance 180 days to sell, and no extension. It came from the leaders of the House’s committee on China, Rep. Mike Gallagher, a Republican, and Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat. The Energy and Commerce Committee voted 50 to 0 for it on March 7, the day it held a classified hearing on TikTok. Then it sat in the Senate. House roll call 86 · H. Rep. 118-417 · Opinion p. 19
Back, inside the foreign aid bill

Seven months from the first petition to a ruling, with no trial and no witnesses.

Straight to the D.C. Circuit, the only court the law allows. Their petition calls a ban “so obviously unconstitutional” that the law’s own sponsors insisted it wasn’t one. The petition said a sale wasn’t “commercially, technologically, or legally feasible” in 270 days, so the law really meant shutting down a platform used by 170 million Americans. Because the law gave the D.C. Circuit exclusive jurisdiction, there was no trial court. The appeals court would decide the case itself, on written evidence. TikTok’s petition ¶¶ 1–2, ¶ 26 · Pub. L. 118-50 § 3

People who make videos on TikTok bring a case of their own, Firebaugh v. Garland. A nonprofit, BASED Politics, follows in June. The law, they said, takes away their right to speak through the publisher they choose and to reach the people who follow them. At both sides’ request, the court sets the briefs for the summer and argument for September. TikTok and the government had asked together for a ruling by December 6, 2024, to leave time for the Supreme Court before the deadline. The court ruled on exactly that day. Joint motion p. 9 · Order of May 28, 2024
The government’s brief, and its secret evidence

The law is about who controls TikTok, not what’s on it, the government says. It asks to file part of its evidence in secret, for the judges alone. Its public evidence was declarations from officials of the intelligence agencies, the FBI and the Justice Department. They described China’s laws requiring companies to help its intelligence work, and a ByteDance tool called Lark that, by the government’s account, employees had used to send US user data to China. The classified parts were blacked out of the copy TikTok got. Government’s D.C. Cir. brief · Motion of Jul 26, 2024
TikTok objects to the secret evidence

It can’t answer what it can’t see, TikTok says, and asks the court to strike the secret filings, or to appoint a special master with clearance to review them. The court never needed to choose. It let the government file the material, and then decided the case without it. TikTok’s opposition, Aug 5, 2024 · D.C. Cir. opinion pp. 64–65

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and Judges Neomi Rao and Douglas Ginsburg hear TikTok, the creators and the government for about two hours. The court had set 50 minutes. Andrew Pincus argued for TikTok, Jeffrey Fisher for the creators, and Daniel Tenny for the government. BASED Politics gave its time to the creators. Judge Ginsburg pressed TikTok on how much of the app is still built in China, reading from TikTok’s own declaration. Chief Judge Srinivasan would later rest his opinion on the long history of limits on foreign control of radio. Minutes, Sept 16, 2024 · Order of Sept 9, 2024 · Argument audio · Tech Policy Press, Sept 17, 2024 · Srinivasan, C.J. pp. 2–5

“The First Amendment exists to protect free speech in the United States,” Judge Ginsburg writes for the court. “Here the Government acted solely to protect that freedom from a foreign adversary nation.” The court said the First Amendment does apply, because TikTok Inc. is “a domestic entity operating domestically,” so “some level of heightened scrutiny is required.” Then it assumed without deciding that the hardest test, strict scrutiny, applied, and found the law passed it anyway, on both of the government’s reasons. It turned down TikTok’s three other claims too. Chief Judge Srinivasan agreed with the result in a concurring opinion, but would have used the middle test, intermediate scrutiny. He ended on what a failed sale would cost. Many Americans “may lose access to an outlet for expression, a source of community, and even a means of income.” D.C. Cir. opinion p. 65, 25, 27, 31 · Srinivasan, C.J. pp. 1, 27 · Judgment, Dec 6, 2024

TikTok asks the court to hold the law off while the Supreme Court looks at it. The same three judges say no. The challengers hadn’t pointed to a single case where a court, after upholding a law, had stopped it from taking effect while the Supreme Court was asked to review it, the judges wrote. The 270 days were “a deliberate choice on the part of the Congress and the President.” The same day, the leaders of the House’s China committee wrote to the heads of Apple and Google to be ready to drop TikTok from their app stores on January 19. Emergency motion, Dec 9, 2024 · Order of Dec 13, 2024 p. 2 · CNBC, Dec 13, 2024
Thirty-two days from TikTok’s first filing to the ruling.

TikTok and the creators each file an emergency application, asking the justices to stop the law from taking effect until they can review it. They asked for an injunction pending review. TikTok had a new lawyer for this court, Noel Francisco, who had been Solicitor General in President Trump’s first term. Application, 24A587 · Application, 24A588 · Jones Day, Francisco
The Court takes the case, in two days

It treats the applications as requests to hear the case, grants them, and sets argument for January 10, nine days before the deadline. It agreed to answer one question, whether the law, “as applied to petitioners, violates the First Amendment.” So TikTok’s other claims, the ones it lost in the D.C. Circuit, were never taken up again. It put off the request to pause the law until after the argument, and gave each side nine days to file its brief and a week to answer the other’s. Docket, No. 24-656 · Opinion p. 2 n. 1

Donald Trump files an amicus brief “supporting neither party,” asking the Court to put the deadline off so he can seek “a negotiated resolution” once he takes office. His lawyer was D. John Sauer, soon to be his Solicitor General. The brief said Trump had 14.7 million followers on TikTok, and that he “alone possesses the consummate dealmaking expertise, the electoral mandate, and the political will” to save the platform. In his first term he had tried to ban it. Trump amicus brief pp. 1–4
TikTok’s brief: a law aimed at speech

Congress singled out one speaker because of what might be said on it, TikTok says, so the hardest test, strict scrutiny, has to apply. TikTok Inc. is an American company, it argued, and choosing which videos to show is its own speech, protected like a newspaper’s choices. It asked the Court to imagine Congress forcing Jeff Bezos to sell the Washington Post because foreign governments might pressure him. The creators filed their own brief the same day. The law, they said, keeps them from working with “the publisher of their choice.” TikTok’s brief pp. 18–23 · Creators’ brief p. 16
The government’s brief: about control, not content

The law deals with the threat “not by imposing any restriction on speech, but instead by prohibiting a foreign adversary from controlling the platform,” the government says. ByteDance is a foreign company abroad with no free-speech rights, it argued, and “a foreign adversary abroad cannot manufacture First Amendment rights for itself by the simple expedient of using an American puppet as a mouthpiece.” Even if the First Amendment applies, it said, the law passes any test, because of China’s data collection on its own, and because China could secretly steer what Americans see. Government’s brief pp. 16–19, 21
TikTok argues: “shut down in nine days”

Noel Francisco opens at 10:08 a.m. Whatever the law is called, he says, “It’s a burden on TikTok’s speech, so the First Amendment applies.” The justices came at him hard. Chief Justice Roberts asked if they were “supposed to ignore the fact that the ultimate parent is, in fact, subject to doing intelligence work for the Chinese government.” Justice Barrett said, “The law doesn’t say TikTok has to shut down. It says ByteDance has to divest.” Justice Kavanaugh called the data collection “a huge concern for the future of the country.” Francisco’s answer was a narrower law that would just bar TikTok Inc. from sharing users’ sensitive data with anyone. Asked what happens on January 19 if TikTok loses, he said, “we go dark.” Tr. pp. 4–6, 8–9, 55–57, 59
The creators argue: “not what we do in this country”

Jeffrey Fisher says the law restricts American creators’ speech because of ideas the government fears, and the First Amendment doesn’t allow that. “Mere ideas do not constitute a national security threat,” he said. He granted that protecting data “is compelling,” but said this law can’t stand on that alone. Chief Justice Roberts pushed back. “Congress doesn’t care about what’s on TikTok,” he said. “They’re saying that the Chinese have to stop controlling TikTok.” Tr. pp. 73–75, 80–82

Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar says China could use TikTok’s data on Americans for “harassment, recruitment, and espionage,” and could secretly steer what they see. Justice Gorsuch asked if worrying about what China might push was “a pretty paternalistic point of view,” when the usual answer to bad speech is more speech. Justice Kagan wondered what “covert” added, since “everybody does know now that there’s China behind it.” The January 19 deadline was “not irrevocable,” Prelogar said. A shutdown “might be just the jolt” ByteDance needed to sell. Justice Sotomayor got her to agree that if TikTok wasn’t cut off on the 19th, the law would be broken. Tr. pp. 117–118, 123–124, 150–151, 171

In rebuttal, Francisco asks again for at least a pause. The argument ends at 12:38 p.m., half an hour past the two hours it was given. A ban on sharing users’ data, or a warning label, would have done the job with less, he said. “If the First Amendment means anything, it means that the government cannot restrict speech in order to protect us from speech.” Tr. pp. 172–178

Two days before the deadline, the Court rules in an unsigned opinion that the law doesn’t violate the First Amendment, at least as it applies to TikTok and the creators. It assumed, without deciding, that the First Amendment applies. Then it found the law content-neutral, so only the middle test applied, and found that keeping China from collecting data on 170 million Americans was reason enough on its own. It didn’t rest on the other reason, covert content manipulation, and it didn’t use the classified evidence. Justice Sotomayor agreed, but would have said plainly that the First Amendment applies. Justice Gorsuch agreed with the result only, noting the Court had had “a fortnight.” The same day it dismissed the requests to pause the law as moot. Opinion pp. 1–2, 9, 13, 18–20 · Sotomayor, J. p. 1 · Gorsuch, J. p. 1 · Journal p. 313
Four days: the ruling, the app going dark, the app coming back, and a new President.
TikTok says it will go dark

Without a clear promise that the law won’t be enforced, TikTok says, it will shut off on January 19. The White House says it’s leaving that to the next one. The Biden administration said enforcement “will be up to the next administration to implement,” and called TikTok’s threat a “stunt.” TikTok said that wasn’t enough for the app stores and web hosts, which are the ones the law would fine. The Verge, Jan 18, 2025 · The Verge, Jan 19, 2025

At about 10:30 p.m. Eastern on Saturday, the app stops working in the US. It’s gone from Apple’s and Google’s app stores too. “Sorry, TikTok isn’t available right now,” the app said. “A law banning TikTok has been enacted in the U.S.” It added that President Trump “has indicated that he will work with us on a solution to reinstate TikTok once he takes office.” ByteDance’s other US apps, like CapCut and Lemon8, went offline too. The Verge, Jan 18, 2025

After Trump says he’ll delay the law and that companies face “no liability,” TikTok comes back around noon Eastern on Sunday. It’s still missing from the app stores. “As a result of President Trump’s efforts, TikTok is back in the U.S.!” the app told users. Its hosting and network companies, Oracle and Akamai, had restored service, relying on his promise. Apple and Google didn’t, yet. The Verge, Jan 19, 2025 · The Verge, Jan 24, 2025

On his first day in office, President Trump orders the Attorney General not to enforce the law for 75 days, and not to punish anyone for the days already passed. The law’s timing, “one day before I took office,” got in the way of his assessing it, the order said. It told the Attorney General to write to each company “that there has been no violation of the statute,” and called any attempt by states or private parties to enforce it “an encroachment on the powers of the Executive.” It didn’t use the law’s own extension, which needed a sale in sight. It was non-enforcement, and the challengers in Tan v. Trump say the law doesn’t allow it. EO 14166 · Amended petition ¶ 2
The law stayed on the books, and the date kept moving.
Letters to Apple, Google and the rest

The Justice Department writes to Apple, Google, Oracle and seven other companies the law would fine, promising they won’t be held responsible. Acting Attorney General James McHenry sent the first round on January 30, and Attorney General Pamela Bondi more after that, including on April 5. The letters said the department would even step in against anyone else who tried to enforce the law. They weren’t public. Zhaocheng Anthony Tan, a Google shareholder, sued for them under FOIA and they came out in July 2025. In 2026 he’d sue over the sale itself. The Verge, Jul 3, 2025

Apple and Google put TikTok back, almost four weeks after taking it down. They waited for the Attorney General’s assurances. The law put their fine at up to $5,000 for each US user. Gray News, Feb 13, 2025 · The Verge, Apr 4, 2025

The Supreme Court sends its judgment down to the D.C. Circuit, which issues its mandate on February 28. The court case is over. Everything after this card happened outside court, until a new case was filed in 2026. Judgment issued · Mandate, Feb 28, 2025

A second order pushes the date to June 19, the same week the President announces new tariffs on China. The White House had believed a sale was close that week, until China said it wouldn’t approve one without talks on trade and tariffs, the Associated Press reported. ByteDance said “key matters” were still unresolved, and that any deal would need China’s approval. EO 14258 · The Verge, Apr 4, 2025
A third order, to September 17. Like the others, it kept the Attorney General from enforcing the law in the meantime. EO 14310 · EO 14352 § 1
A fourth order, to December 16. Nine days later the President said he had a deal. EO 14350 · EO 14352 § 1
A deal approved, signed, and closed.

He determines that selling TikTok’s US business to a new joint venture, “once its implementation agreements are executed,” is the qualified divestiture the law demands. Under his findings, ByteDance and its affiliates would own less than 20 percent. The new company would control “the algorithms and code” and content moderation, keep US data in a US company’s cloud, and have the recommendation models retrained on US data and watched by “trusted security partners.” Vice President JD Vance led the review. The order gave the deal 120 more days to close, with the law still not enforced. It was the fifth order holding the Attorney General off. EO 14352

TikTok’s chief executive, Shou Zi Chew, tells employees ByteDance has signed with three lead investors, Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX of Abu Dhabi. It will close on January 22. The three would hold 15 percent each, ByteDance just under 20, and existing ByteDance investors about 30, according to the memo. Vice President Vance had put the US business’s value at about $14 billion. The memo also said TikTok’s global companies “will manage global product interoperability and certain commercial activities, including e-commerce, advertising, and marketing.” That line would come back in Tan v. Trump. CNBC, Dec 18, 2025

It says US data is kept in “Oracle’s secure U.S. cloud environment,” and that it “will retrain, test, and update the content recommendation algorithm on U.S. user data.” ByteDance keeps 19.9 percent, and Shou Zi Chew sits on its seven-member board. That night President Trump posted that he was “so happy to have helped in saving TikTok!” Presser and the new company’s chief security officer, Will Farrell, had both signed declarations for TikTok in this case in 2024, about how the app was run and secured. TikTok USDS Joint Venture, Jan 23, 2026 · Reply, Jun 8, 2026 p. 2 · JA 481 · JA 769
A new petition under the same law says the sale breaks it. Nothing in it has been decided.
A new case: Tan v. Trump

Two software engineers, Zhaocheng Anthony Tan and Garrett Reid, petition the D.C. Circuit. The sale, they say, “facially violated the law.” Tan owns stock in Alphabet and Reid in Meta, two of TikTok’s rivals, and their lawyer, Brendan Ballou, is with a group called the Public Integrity Project. They say ByteDance still owns the algorithm and licenses it to the new company, still runs its e-commerce, advertising and marketing, and that TikTok’s global chief executive sits on its board. That’s an operational relationship, they say, which the law forbids. They don’t ask for TikTok to be banned. They ask the court to declare the extensions, the failure to investigate and the sale unlawful, and to order the Attorney General to investigate. Petition, Mar 5, 2026 · Amended petition ¶¶ 2–5, p. 44

An amended petition adds “John Doe,” who says he lost his job at one of ByteDance’s US companies because of the deal. He asked to use a pseudonym because he’s a first-generation Chinese American with family still in China. The petition adds claims that ByteDance staff “continue to demand — and receive — access to aggregated American user data,” and that the two companies jointly launched a feature to track users’ exact GPS locations. These are the challengers’ claims. None of them has been tested in court. Amended petition pp. 3–6

A panel of three judges lets the amended petition in and lets John Doe stay anonymous, but won’t speed the case up for now. The judges, Justin Walker, J. Michelle Childs and Bradley Garcia, told the government to file any motion to end the case by May 21. They put off the challengers’ request to add evidence of their own. Order of Apr 29, 2026
Too late, and no standing, the government says

It asks the court to dismiss the case without getting to the deal at all, for two reasons. First, the deadline to sue. The law allows 90 days after a government action, and the government says the last one was the President’s order of September 25, 2025, so the March 2026 petition “missed by several months.” Second, standing. Owning stock in a rival doesn’t give anyone a right to sue, it says, and the effect on a stock price is “highly speculative.” It hasn’t argued yet whether the sale meets the law. The challengers answer: “a few weeks later”

“The President endorsed, and ByteDance announced, the divestiture of TikTok’s American assets on January 22, 2026,” they say. “Petitioners filed their lawsuit a few weeks later.” The September order only approved a deal “once its implementation agreements are executed,” they argued, so it wasn’t final or ripe until the sale closed. And Reid uses TikTok, so his own data is at stake, they said, while Doe lost his job and the shareholders lost money. Opposition pp. 7–10, 13
The government replies: a post isn’t an order

The only thing that happened in January, it says, was a social media post by the President, and the post “reflects no Presidential action, finding, or determination under the Act.” The post began “I am so happy to have helped in saving TikTok!” and went on to thank China’s President Xi for “ultimately, approving the Deal.” A ruling against a post “would have no practical effect,” the government said, and the challengers’ data theory was “speculation piled upon speculation.” Reply pp. 1–3
Government phones can have it again

The Justice Department’s lawyers decide the 2022 ban on government devices doesn’t cover the new TikTok. The new company “functions independently of ByteDance, is majority-owned by American investors, and has revised the content-recommendation algorithm and cybersecurity program,” the opinion said. The department had given the White House the same advice, at first on conditions, in February and March. OLC opinion, Jul 16, 2026

Two judges send the government’s motion to dismiss on to the judges who will decide the whole case, the merits panel. So whether the challengers sued in time, and whether they can sue at all, will be decided along with everything else, after full briefing. The two sides were told to propose how the case should go on. Order of Jul 20, 2026

On a joint motion to govern, the clerk gives the government until October 20, 2026 to file the certified index of the record. After that the two sides would propose a schedule for briefs. Both kept their objections, the challengers to what the record leaves out and the government to their adding evidence of their own. Joint motion, Aug 19, 2026 · Order of Aug 21, 2026
